content: The elimination of amlodipine from plasma occurs in a biphasic manner, with a terminal elimination half-life of approximately 30 to 50 hours. Steady-state plasma concentrations of amlodipine are achieved after 7 to 8 days of consistent daily dosing. The pharmacokinetics of amlodipine are not significantly affected by renal impairment. Therefore, patients with renal failure can be administered the usual initial dose without the need for adjustment. In elderly patients and those with hepatic insufficiency, the clearance of amlodipine is reduced, leading to an increase in the area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) by approximately 40–60%. As a result, a lower initial dose may be necessary. A similar increase in AUC has been observed in patients with moderate to severe heart failure. Weight-adjusted clearance and volume of distribution of amlodipine in pediatric patients are comparable to those observed in adults. Long-term studies in animals, using doses up to 5 mg/kg/day, have shown no evidence of carcinogenicity. Mutagenicity studies with amlodipine maleate have revealed no drug-related effects at either the gene or chromosome level. Additionally, no adverse effects on fertility were observed in rats treated with oral amlodipine maleate at doses up to 10 mg/kg/day, which is approximately eight times the maximum recommended human dose on a mg/m² basis. The antihypertensive efficacy of amlodipine besylate has been demonstrated in 15 double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized studies involving 800 patients treated with amlodipine and 538 patients receiving placebo. Once-daily administration of amlodipine resulted in statistically significant reductions in both supine and standing blood pressures at 24 hours post-dose. The average reductions were approximately 12/6 mmHg in the standing position and 13/7 mmHg in the supine position in patients with mild to moderate hypertension. The blood pressure-lowering effect was maintained throughout the 24-hour dosing interval, with minimal differences between peak and trough effects. No evidence of tolerance was observed in patients studied for up to one year. Dose-response studies demonstrated that reductions in blood pressure were dose-related within the recommended dosing range. The effects on diastolic pressure were similar in younger and older patients, while the reduction in systolic pressure was greater in older patients, likely due to higher baseline systolic pressures. The antihypertensive effects were consistent across racial groups, including Black and White patients. In patients with chronic stable angina, the effectiveness of amlodipine at doses of 5 to 10 mg/day has been evaluated in eight placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trials lasting up to six weeks and involving 1,038 patients (684 treated with amlodipine and 354 with placebo). In five of these studies, significant increases in exercise duration (on bicycle or treadmill) were observed with the 10 mg dose. Amlodipine 10 mg also increased the time to 1 mm ST-segment depression in several studies and reduced the frequency of angina attacks. The sustained efficacy of amlodipine in angina patients has been demonstrated with long-term dosing. In the PREVENT study, 825 patients with angiographically documented coronary artery disease (CAD) were randomized to receive amlodipine (5 to 10 mg once daily) or placebo for three years. Although the study did not achieve statistical significance for its primary endpoint (change in coronary luminal diameter assessed by quantitative coronary angiography), the data suggested a favorable outcome in terms of fewer hospitalizations for angina and revascularization procedures in patients with CAD. In the CAMELOT study, 1,318 patients with recently documented CAD (via angiography) but without left main coronary disease, heart failure, or an ejection fraction <40% were randomized to double-blind treatment with either amlodipine (5 to 10 mg once daily) or placebo in addition to standard care. Standard care included aspirin (89%), statins (83%), beta-blockers (74%), nitroglycerin (50%), anticoagulants (40%), and diuretics (32%), but excluded other calcium channel blockers. The mean follow-up duration was 19 months.
